earliest_print_source: "What Constitutes Success?" (contest-winning definition), Bessie Anderson Stanley, 1904/1905
notes: This is a variant of the widely circulated "Success" passage whose documented origin is Bessie Anderson Stanley's 1904 prize-winning entry, published 1905: "He has achieved success who has lived well, laughed often, and loved much..." The phrase "laughed often, and loved much" here is verbatim Stanley; "worked well" is the drifted opening. This text is most famously misattributed to Emerson, and secondarily to Elbert Hubbard. I hold the Stanley origin with reasonable confidence, but I cannot rule out that Hubbard separately published a variant of his own in The Philistine or his epigram collections, which would make this a genuine-Hubbard rewording rather than a clean misattribution. Flagging for human review rather than asserting either way at high confidence.

One of the most-repeated Eleanor Roosevelt lines and one of the least supported. It does not appear in her books, her "My Day" columns, or her speeches as far as I know, and researchers who have gone looking (Wikiquote's disputed/misattributed section, Quote Investigator) place the earliest attributions decades after her 1962 death. I have no identifiable true author, so I am not offering a reattribution. Should not be promoted.

earliest_print_source: Reader's Digest, September 1940 (quoted as Eleanor Roosevelt)
notes: Better supported than most ER attributions but still not primary. The standard earliest citation is a 1940 Reader's Digest quotation credited to her during her lifetime, which she is not known to have disputed; her 1937 autobiography "This Is My Story" contains related material about inferiority but not this sentence. So: attributed in her lifetime, never located in her own writing. I am fairly but not fully confident of the Reader's Digest 1940 detail. The "Remember" at the start of the input text is an addition to the standard wording.

earliest_print_source: You Learn by Living, Eleanor Roosevelt, 1960
notes: Genuine and sourced. From the chapter on fear in "You Learn by Living" (1960): "You gain strength, courage, and confidence by every experience in which you really stop to look fear in the face... You must do the thing you think you cannot do." This is the rare ER quotation with a real primary source in her own book.
